newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Race starts for Taiwan mobile phone licences.
newsitem.headline: Race starts for Taiwan mobile phone licences.

text.p: The race for Taiwan's potentially rich mobile telephone market was under way on Tuesday with the closing of applications for government licences.
The Taiwanese government said 17 joint ventures have submitted applications for eight mobile phone operation licences in the recently deregulated market.
"The application deadline was September 30, and we are not accepting any more as of today," an official from the Ministry of Transportation and Communication said by telephone.
The official, who asked not to be named, said a special screening committee under the ministry would finish reviewing the applications by the end of 1996.
The official declined to give the names of the companies.
"The government has to protect the names of the bidders in order to ensure impartiality in the screening process," the official said.
Major domestic and foreign firms had confirmed earlier their plans to apply for the lucrative licenses.

Taiwan's Koo's Group said it had signed agreements with U.S. Sprint Corp and Microelectronics Technology to launch a mobile phone joint venture. Air Touch Communications Inc and Walsin Lihwa Corp had confirmed they were partners in a T$6 billion (US$218 million) venture.

Other previously declared applicants included Japan's Mitsubishi in an eight-partner venture with Taiwan's Tung Ho Steel, Singapore Telecommunications with Taiwan's Aurora Corp, Hong Kong Telecommunications, and Pacific Electric Wire and Cable with Acer Inc.
Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp also has said it was considering to launch a venture.

The mobile telephone sector is one of several telecom sectors liberalised by the parliament in January, opening them up to private and limited foreign investment. Foreign investors can own stakes of up to 20 percent in Taiwan telecom ventures.
It is expected to be the most lucrative of the liberalised sectors, with analysts forecasting sales of T$18.7 billion (US$680 million) for the next 10 years.

"The sector is where investors and financial markets will be focusing attention for the next couple of months, because this is the biggest chunk of the new telecommunication pie," said Oliver Fang, senior analyst at National Securities.
Other liberalised sectors were paging systems, trunking radio and mobile data.
The expected huge size of the market has aroused concerns that influence-peddling and corruption may taint the bidding process.
The ministry official admitted that the government was worried about potential attempts by gangsters to influence the screening of licences.
"Obviously the interference of any outside forces has to be a concern that we must protect ourselves against," he said.
